kierkegaard-anxiety: Anxiety, in Søren Kierkegaard's analysis, is the peculiar unease that arises when a person confronts their own freedom and the open range of what they might become. Unlike fear, which has a definite object, anxiety has no object; it is the dizziness we feel gazing into the abyss of possibility, aware that we could choose otherwise. Kierkegaard treats it not as a mere pathology but as a defining mark of the self, bound up with the awareness of sin and the demand to become an individual before God.
teleological-suspension: The teleological suspension of the ethical is Kierkegaard's provocative claim that faith can, in rare cases, require setting aside universal moral duty for the sake of a higher relation to the divine. His central example is Abraham, commanded to sacrifice Isaac, whose obedience makes no sense within ordinary ethics and can be justified only by a private, absolute duty to God. The idea dramatizes the gap between the ethical, which is universal and communicable, and faith, which is singular and cannot be fully explained to others.
subjective-truth: With the phrase "subjectivity is truth," Kierkegaard argues that for the deepest existential matters what counts is not objective correctness but the passion and inwardness with which one holds and lives a belief. He distinguishes truths that can be established impersonally from truths, especially religious ones, whose meaning depends on how they are appropriated by an existing individual. The claim is not that facts are relative but that certain truths become real only through committed, personal engagement rather than detached observation.
intentionality: Intentionality is the feature of consciousness by which every mental act is directed at or about something: perceiving is perceiving of an object, believing is believing that something is the case. Revived by Franz Brentano and made central by Edmund Husserl, the notion holds that this "aboutness" is the essential mark distinguishing the mental from the merely physical. For phenomenology it becomes the guiding thread of analysis, since to study consciousness is to study the structured ways it intends its objects.
phenomenology: Phenomenology is the philosophical study of experience as it is lived and given to consciousness, aiming to describe the structures of appearance rather than to explain them causally. Inaugurated as a rigorous method by Edmund Husserl, it asks us to set aside assumptions about the external world—the so-called bracketing or epoché—so as to attend to phenomena precisely as they present themselves. Later thinkers such as Heidegger, Sartre, and Merleau-Ponty extended it toward questions of existence, embodiment, and being, making it one of the most influential movements of twentieth-century thought.
dasein: Dasein, literally "being-there," is Martin Heidegger's term for the kind of being that we ourselves are—the entity for whom its own existence is at issue and who has an implicit understanding of what it means to be. Rather than treating the human as a substance or thinking subject, Heidegger analyzes Dasein through the ways it is always already involved in a world, engaged with things and others. The concept reframes the study of the human around care, temporality, and the question of Being itself.
being-toward-death: Being-toward-death is Heidegger's account of how mortality shapes human existence not as a distant event but as an ever-present possibility that structures how we live. Because death is one's own, certain, and cannot be delegated to anyone else, honestly facing it individualizes a person and can pull them out of anonymous everyday distraction. Anticipating death, on this view, is not morbid but a condition for grasping one's life as a finite, unified whole and living it authentically.
authenticity: Authenticity, in Heidegger's sense, names a way of existing in which one takes ownership of one's own possibilities rather than drifting along in the anonymous patterns dictated by "the they." It is achieved not by escaping the social world but by resolutely owning one's finitude and choosing in light of it, as against the inauthentic tendency to lose oneself in conventional expectations. The term is descriptive rather than moralistic, marking a difference in how existence is enacted rather than a code of correct behavior.
thrownness: Thrownness, Heidegger's Geworfenheit, captures the fact that we always find ourselves already delivered into a situation we did not choose: a time, place, body, language, culture, and set of circumstances. We do not create the conditions of our existence but are "thrown" into them, and this facticity is the background against which any freedom or projection of possibilities takes place. The notion emphasizes that human existence is finite and situated, never a blank starting point.
das-man: The they-self, or das Man, is Heidegger's name for the anonymous "one" that governs much of everyday life—as in what "one" does, says, or thinks—into which individuals typically dissolve. In this mode people conform to averaged expectations, letting public opinion decide their choices and thereby covering over their own responsibility for existence. Heidegger regards this as the ordinary, largely inauthentic condition of Dasein, from which authentic selfhood must be won back rather than presupposed.
heidegger-technology: In his reflections on technology, Heidegger argues that its essence is not any particular machine or tool but a mode of disclosure he calls "enframing," in which everything shows up as a stockpile of resources to be ordered and exploited. Modern technology thus reveals nature and even human beings as mere "standing-reserve," narrowing our sense of what things are. Heidegger warns that this way of seeing is dangerous because it threatens to conceal other, richer relations to the world, yet he suggests that recognizing it may also open a path toward a freer relationship with technology.
existence-precedes-essence: "Existence precedes essence" is Jean-Paul Sartre's slogan for the core of atheistic existentialism: there is no fixed human nature given in advance, so a person first exists and only afterward defines what they are through their choices. Unlike a manufactured object whose purpose is set before it is made, the human being arrives without a predetermined role and must create meaning and value through action. This places the full weight of self-definition, and hence responsibility, on the individual.
bad-faith: Bad faith is Sartre's term for the self-deception by which we flee from our own freedom, pretending to be fixed things rather than the free beings we are. A person in bad faith might treat their social role, past, or circumstances as an unchangeable essence in order to disown the responsibility of choosing. Sartre illustrates it with figures like the waiter overplaying his role, showing how we lie to ourselves to escape the anxiety of radical freedom.
sartre-freedom: For Sartre, human beings are radically free and therefore wholly responsible, "condemned to be free" because we cannot avoid choosing even when we try. Since no God, nature, or external authority determines our values, every action is a self-defining commitment, and in choosing for ourselves we implicitly affirm an image of what a human being should be. This freedom is not liberating comfort but a heavy burden, inseparable from anguish and the impossibility of blaming circumstances for who we become.
the-look: The Look is Sartre's analysis of what happens when another person's gaze turns me into an object in their world, revealing that I exist not only for myself but also for others. Being seen can bring shame or self-consciousness, because the other apprehends me as a fixed thing over which I have no control, and I in turn objectify them. This conflict of freedoms lies behind the famous line "hell is other people," expressing how our being is perpetually contested in the presence of other subjects.
